cards.explanation: The answer is the grace of God, friends. Paul says he acted in holiness and sincerity that are from God, not in worldly wisdom, but in the grace of God (2 Corinthians 1:12). Look at that. The man is boasting, and the credit still goes straight to God. That's how you know it's a healthy boast.

The answer is False, friends. Paul says, “…we do not write you anything that is beyond your ability to read and understand.” (2 Corinthians 1:13). What he writes, they can read and understand. I respect that, because my recipes have been called a lot of things, and readable is not always one of them.

The answer is boast of each other, friends! Paul hopes they'll understand him completely, so that they may boast of him just as he will boast of them in the day of our Lord Jesus (2 Corinthians 1:13-14). That's a two-way street. Everybody's proud of everybody. It's a good picture of what church can look like.

The word is double, friends! Paul planned to visit first so the Corinthians might receive a double blessing (2 Corinthians 1:15). That fits his plan to see them on the way to Macedonia and again on the way back (2 Corinthians 1:16). Double the visits, double the blessing. If a bakery gave me a double batch I'd stand on this base and cheer.

The answer is Judea, friends. Paul wanted to visit Corinth on his way to Macedonia, return from Macedonia, and then have the Corinthians help him on his way to Judea (2 Corinthians 1:16). So Corinth was meant to send him off. That's a church doing some serious travel support.

The answer is False, friends. Paul says as surely as God is faithful, his message to the Corinthians is not “Yes” and “No” (2 Corinthians 1:18). No flip-flopping on the message. The plans may change, but what he preaches stays put.

The answer is all, friends! Paul says all the promises of God are “Yes” in Christ (2 Corinthians 1:20). Not a handful, not the easy ones. Every single one, and that's why he says our “Amen” goes up through Him to the glory of God. That's a whole lot of Yes.

The answer is True, friends! Paul writes that God “…placed His seal on us…” (2 Corinthians 1:22). Right next to that, he says God anointed them and put His Spirit in their hearts (2 Corinthians 1:21-22). That's three things God did, stacked one right after another, and Paul isn't slowing down.

The answer is His Spirit, friends. Paul says God “…put His Spirit in our hearts as a pledge of what is to come.” (2 Corinthians 1:22). The Spirit is the pledge, a guarantee of what is to come. The Spirit is in their hearts now, and what is to come is still ahead.

The answer is to spare the church, friends. Paul calls God as his witness that it was to spare them that he didn't return to Corinth (2 Corinthians 1:23). He takes it that seriously. When a man swears this way, you don't need to read between the lines.

The word is workers, friends! Paul says they don't lord it over the church's faith. They're fellow workers with the Corinthians for their joy (2 Corinthians 1:24). That puts everybody in the same kitchen, sleeves up. I like a boss who picks up a whisk.

The word is painful, friends. Paul says he made up his mind not to make another painful visit (2 Corinthians 2:1). That tells us a painful visit already happened. He's choosing a different way this time.

The answer is those he grieved, friends. Paul asks, if he grieves the Corinthians, who is left to cheer him but those whom he has grieved? (2 Corinthians 2:2). So the ones he names are the very people he would have grieved. Their joy matters to him.

The answer is True, friends. Paul says he wrote so that on his arrival he would not be grieved by those who ought to make him rejoice (2 Corinthians 2:3). He also says he had confidence in all of them, that they'd share his joy. He's hoping for a good reunion.

The answer is how much he loves them, friends. Paul says he wrote through many tears out of great distress and anguish of heart, “…not to grieve you but to let you know how much I love you.” (2 Corinthians 2:4). That's a heavy letter, written by a man who cares. I think it hurt him to write it.

The answer is False, friends. Paul says anyone who has caused grief has not grieved him but all of the Corinthians, to some degree, not to overstate it (2 Corinthians 2:5). So the hurt belonged to the whole church. And notice Paul is careful here, not piling it on.

The answer is forgive and comfort him, friends. Paul says, “…you ought to forgive and comfort him…” (2 Corinthians 2:7). He says the punishment imposed by the majority is sufficient (2 Corinthians 2:6). So mercy is what comes next, so that the man will not be overwhelmed by excessive sorrow.

The word is sorrow, friends. Paul says they should forgive and comfort him “…so that he will not be overwhelmed by excessive sorrow.” (2 Corinthians 2:7). So even after punishment, there's a limit. Paul doesn't want him buried.

The word is obedient, friends. Paul says his purpose in writing was to see if they would “…stand the test and be obedient in everything.” (2 Corinthians 2:9). So he wrote to see how they would do. And I think he's hoping they pass.

The answer is Christ, friends. Paul says that if he has forgiven anything, he has forgiven it in the presence of Christ for their sake (2 Corinthians 2:10). So Christ is the one in whose presence he forgives. The church is who it's for.

The answer is Satan, friends. Paul says he forgives in order that Satan should not outwit them, and adds, “…we are not unaware of his schemes.” (2 Corinthians 2:10-11). So his forgiving is tied to Satan not outwitting them. It's a serious line, and Paul says it plainly.
